summary: Describes the structure and identification of management information for TCP/IP-based internets, the rules for how managed items are named and defined. It is a re-release of RFC 1065 with a changed status section and typo fixes. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices from different vendors can only be managed together if everyone agrees on how each reported item is named and what kind of value it holds. RFC 1155 defines that shared naming scheme and those value types, and it is the foundation that SNMP management information is built on.

questions: what is the structure of management information
what is the 1.3.6.1 object identifier prefix
what are snmp counter and gauge types
subtitle: The naming scheme and building blocks that every SNMP-managed device uses to describe what it can report.

tldr.problem: To manage devices from many vendors, everyone must agree on how each managed item is named, what kind of value it holds and how its definition is written down.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1155 names every managed object with an OBJECT IDENTIFIER on a global tree rooted at the internet prefix 1.3.6.1, limits the ASN.1 types that may be used, and defines a standard OBJECT-TYPE format for describing objects.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that re-releases RFC 1065 with a changed status section and typo fixes, and it leaves the actual objects to the MIB memo and the protocol to the SNMP memo.

today: RFC 1155 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1065, whose technical content it carries unchanged, and it remains the base structure and identification scheme for TCP/IP management information.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1155 describes the common structures and identification scheme used to define management information for TCP/IP-based internets. It gives an object information model and a set of generic types, written down formally in Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1).

The memo is largely concerned with organizational concerns and administrative policy. It neither specifies the objects that are managed nor the protocols used to manage them. Those jobs belong to two companion memos: RFC 1156 for the Management Information Base (MIB) and RFC 1157 for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

Its two goals are simplicity and extensibility. The authors state that understanding of internet management was not yet complete, so a simple SMI imposes the fewest constraints on future approaches, and an extensible one leaves the most room for experiments. It differs from an earlier IETF working note in one big way: that note focused entirely on OSI-style network management and so was not suitable for use with SNMP.

The memo specifies a Standard Protocol with the status Recommended. The Internet Activities Board recommends that all IP and TCP implementations be network manageable, which implies the Internet MIB and at least one of SNMP or CMOT.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not say which values to measure or which protocol to ask with. It only fixes how managed items get their names and what kinds of values they can hold, so the companion memos can build on it.

sections.title: Naming Objects with OBJECT IDENTIFIERs
sections.content:
Each type of managed object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is a unique OBJECT IDENTIFIER: a sequence of integers that traverses a global tree. Each node has a label pairing a brief textual description with an integer, and administrative control of the meanings assigned to nodes may be delegated as one traverses the tree.

Under the unlabeled root sit three children: ccitt(0), administered by the International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee; iso(1), administered by the International Organization for Standardization; and joint-iso-ccitt(2), jointly administered. Under iso sits org(3) for other international organizations, and one of its subtrees was transferred by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology to the U.S. Department of Defense, dod(6).

The memo assumes the Department of Defense will allocate a node to the Internet community, administered by the Internet Activities Board: internet ::= { iso org(3) dod(6) 1 }, the prefix 1.3.6.1. Four subtrees start under internet:

  • directory(1): reserved for a future memo on using the OSI Directory in the Internet.
  • mgmt(2): objects defined in IAB-approved documents. The initial Internet-standard MIB would be management document number 1, using { mgmt 1 }, or 1.3.6.1.2.1.
  • experimental(3): objects used in Internet experiments. An experimenter given number 17 would use 1.3.6.1.3.17.
  • private(4): objects defined unilaterally. It holds enterprises(1), where vendors can register models of their products.

The IAB delegates administration of mgmt, experimental and private to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. The memo's own example is a made-up company numbered 1.3.6.1.4.1.42 registering a product at 1.3.6.1.4.1.42.1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Every managed item gets an address on a giant numbered family tree. The address is a list of branch numbers from the top, and different organizations look after different branches.

sections.title: Allowed Syntax and Defined Types
sections.content:
To keep things simple, the memo allows only part of ASN.1. The permitted primitive types are INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER and NULL. If an enumerated INTEGER is used, a named number with the value 0 must not appear in the list of enumerations.

The constructor type SEQUENCE is allowed only to build lists or tables. A list is a fixed set of primitive fields that are always present, with no DEFAULT or OPTIONAL clauses. A table is a SEQUENCE OF an entry that is itself a list.

The memo also defines application-wide types that resolve into implicit primitives, lists, tables or other application-wide types:

  • NetworkAddress: a CHOICE among protocol families; only the Internet family is present.
  • IpAddress: a 32-bit internet address, an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order, encoded with the primitive form of the ASN.1 basic encoding rules.
  • Counter: a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it wraps to zero after its maximum of 4294967295.
  • Gauge: a non-negative integer that may increase or decrease but latches at the maximum of 4294967295.
  • TimeTicks: a non-negative integer counting hundredths of a second since an epoch that each object's description names.
  • Opaque: an arbitrary ASN.1 value encoded to octets and then wrapped again as an OCTET STRING, in effect double-wrapping it. A conforming implementation need only accept and recognize such data, not unwrap it.

Values are carried on the network by applying the ASN.1 basic encoding rules to the object's syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo hands out a small box of building blocks: whole numbers, text, addresses, counters that only go up, and gauges that rise and fall but stop at a ceiling. You may build only with those blocks.

sections.title: Defining Managed Objects
sections.content:
The memo does not define MIB objects itself, but it fixes the format other memos must use. An object type definition has five fields: OBJECT (a textual OBJECT DESCRIPTOR and its OBJECT IDENTIFIER), Syntax, Definition, Access (read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible) and Status (mandatory, optional or obsolete).

No object type in the Internet-standard MIB may use a sub-identifier of 0 in its name, because that value is reserved for future extensions. Each OBJECT DESCRIPTOR must be a unique, mnemonic, printable string, which promotes a common language for humans discussing the MIB.

The memo separates an object type, a declarative definition of a kind of managed object, from an object instance, a type bound to a value. A list type groups several simple types; a table is a SEQUENCE OF a list type. The worked example is an address translation table whose entries hold atIndex, atPhysAddress and atNetAddress.

How instances are referenced is left to each management protocol, which must also say which instances come back when a request matches more than one. To help tools process definitions, the OBJECT-TYPE macro captures the SYNTAX, ACCESS and STATUS of an object formally.
sections.plainLanguage: Every managed item gets a standard form to fill in: its name, what kind of answer it gives, what it means, whether you may change it and whether it is still in use. The same form everywhere keeps definitions tidy and machine-readable.

sections.title: Extending the MIB Over Time
sections.content:
Every Internet-standard MIB document obsoletes all earlier ones. The portion of a name, called the tail, that follows the OBJECT IDENTIFIER { mgmt version-number } must remain unchanged between versions.

New versions may declare old object types obsolete (but not delete their names), append non-aggregate object types to a list type, or define entirely new object types. They may not change the semantics of any previously defined object without changing that object's name.

These rules let several MIB versions share the same tail-space, which greatly simplifies implementations that support more than one version. The price is that a management agent might return an instance that is a superset of the expected object type. Following the principle of robustness, a manager should ignore the extra information. For control actions the rule is stricter: if an instance does not have the same syntax as its expected object type, the action must fail. In every case, the name of an object returned by an operation must be identical to the name requested.
sections.plainLanguage: When the rulebook gets a new edition, old names keep their meanings. You may add new items, but you may not quietly change what an old name means, and old names are never deleted.

sections.title: Status and Security Notes
sections.content:
RFC 1155 is a re-release of RFC 1065 with a changed Status of this Memo and a few minor typographical corrections; the technical content is unchanged. It specifies a Standard Protocol with the status Recommended, and the Internet Activities Board recommends that all IP and TCP implementations be network manageable. That implies implementation of the Internet MIB (RFC 1156) and at least one of the management protocols SNMP (RFC 1157) or CMOT (RFC 1095). At the time of writing, SNMP is a full Internet standard and CMOT is a draft standard.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a second printing of an earlier rulebook with small fixes and an updated status section. It says nothing about keeping management data safe.
